# Data Types and Variables
In programming languages different types of data can be used. The most common types are:

- Integer numbers (e.g. 1, 2, 3)
- Floating point numbers (e.g. 1.0, 2.0, 3.0)
- Characters (e.g. 'a', 'b', 'c')
- Strings (e.g. "abc", "Hello World")

When you write a code you will be able to define variables and assign values to them. The names of the variablse can be chosen by you (you can use characters, underscores and numbers, but the name should not start with a number). For example:

```{julia}
#| output: false
a = 1
b = 1.0
c = "one"
my_variable_1 = 2.0
my_variable_2 = 3.0
```

In your further code you will be able to use the variables and for example be able to perform calculations with data of the type Integer and Floating point number:

```{julia}
x = a + a
```
```{julia}
y = b + b
```
```{julia}
my_result = my_variable_1 + my_variable_2
```
# Basic Functions

If you forgot the data type of one of your variables you can use `typeof()` to check it:

```{julia}
typeof(a)
```
```{julia}
typeof(b)
```
```{julia}
typeof(c)
```
Below the code box with `typeof()` you can see the output Int64. This means that the type of a is a signed integer that is represented by 64 bits. There is also the possibility to have other data types e.g. Int32. The difference between these two Integer types is the number of bits used for representing them. If more bits are used to represent the Integer, a broader range of storable values can be covered. An Int32 could be used for a range of -2147483648 to 2147483648 while an Int64 could be used for a range of -9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775808. 

By writing `typeof()` you are using a function. You can regognize a function by the parentheses `()` after the name of the function. Functions can take arguments, which will be placed inside the parentheses, and return values. In this case, the argument is the variable you want to check the type of and the return value is the type of data. You can also see that the color of the name of the function and the parentheses are written in a different color than the rest of the code. This is called syntax highlighting and it helps you to read the code easier.

There is also a function which can be used to check the size of the data. This function can be used by tiping `sizeof()`. Like `typeof()` this function takes an argument and returns a value. The argument is the variable you want to check the size of and the return value is the size of the data in bytes. Note that there is also the function `size()`, that will for example take an vector as argument and return the size of the vector with regard to its elements.
```{julia}
sizeof(a)
```
```{julia}
sizeof(b)
```
```{julia}
sizeof(c)
```
With functions you can also perform many simple mathematical operations such as:

- `abs(x)`    which calculates the absolute value of x
- `sqrt(x)`   which calculates the square root of x
- `log(x)`    which calculates the natural logarithm of x
- `log10(x)`  which calculates the logarithm with base 10 of x
- `exp(x)`    which calculates the natural exponantial function with x in the exponent

And the trigonometric functions for calculations with degrees:

- `sind(x)`, `cosd(x)`, `tand(x)`
- `asind(x)`, `acosd(x)`, `atand(x)` 

and with radians: 

- `sin(x)`, `cos(x)`, `tan(x)`
- `asin(x)`, `acos(x)`, `atan(x)` 

The basic arithmetic operators `+`, `-`, `*` and `\` are also functions, but they are written in a different way.

# Try it on Your Own
Go to Your Editor (e.g. VSCode) or Google Colab and create a new .IPYNB file (Jupyter Notebook), add a new code cell and define some Variables. Use the `typeof()` function and the `sizeof()` function to check the type and the size of your variables. After that try to perform some basic arethmetic operations like `+`, `-`, `*` and `\` with your variables.
